blocks.text: The chapter contrasts two outcomes associated with the coming Day: the proud and those who do evil are pictured as stubble consumed by fire, while those who fear the Lord’s name receive vindication, healing, and freedom. The “sun of righteousness” is a solar image for restoration; later claims that identify it as a particular person go beyond the image itself. The closing appeal remembers Moses’ Torah—God’s instructions, statutes, and judgments for Israel—and promises Elijah before the Day. Some interpreters understand this Moses-and-Elijah conclusion as linking Torah and prophecy and possibly reflecting the shaping of Malachi’s ending and the Book of the Twelve.

The promised turning of parents’ hearts toward children and children’s hearts toward parents belongs to Malachi’s own Persian-period setting, where temple life, kinship, agriculture, and covenant disputes formed part of the book’s concerns. That setting should be distinguished from later institutions and relationships when interpreting or applying these verses.
